Sustainable agriculture means farming in a way that keeps your land able to feed you and earn for you next year, in ten years and when your children take over. It is not a special label or a costly system. It is a set of habits that **put back what each harvest takes out**, protect the soil from sun and rain, and use water carefully.
A farmer working in a green field
Every practice in this course aims at one thing: a field that keeps producing season after season.
Why yields fall without any disaster

Every bag of maize, every basket of tomatoes and every heap of yams you carry away contains nitrogen, phosphorus, potassium and other nutrients that came from your soil. When stalks are burnt and nothing is returned, the soil gets a little poorer each season. Rain then washes bare topsoil away, and the hot sun burns off the **organic matter**, the dark, crumbly remains of plants and animals that hold water and feed soil life. The result is a slow slide: more fertiliser for the same harvest, harder ground, and crops that wilt quickly in a dry spell.

Soil is alive. A handful of healthy soil holds earthworms, termites, fungi and billions of bacteria. Some bacteria, called **rhizobia**, live in small lumps (nodules) on the roots of legumes such as cowpea, groundnut and soybean, and turn nitrogen from the air into a form plants can use. Fungi spread thin threads that help roots reach water and phosphorus. When you feed and protect this underground workforce, it works for you for free.

Sustainable farming also looks beyond the soil. It protects water by stopping runoff and wasteful irrigation, protects the insects and birds that pollinate crops and eat pests, and protects your family by cutting careless pesticide use. On a small farm these goals usually point the same way: a covered, living soil holds more rain, grows stronger plants and needs fewer costly rescues.

The three principles of conservation agriculture

Many poor soils in Nigeria need some mineral fertiliser to give a decent yield. Sustainable farming uses compost, legumes and mulch so that every bag of fertiliser you buy works harder and less is wasted. The aim is healthy soil and a fair profit, not a slogan.

Worked example: is the soil being run down?
For example, Amina farms 1 hectare of maize near Zaria. She burns the stalks every dry season and writes down her fertiliser and harvest each year.
Year 1: she used 4 bags (50 kg each) of NPK and harvested 40 bags (100 kg each) of maize. That is 40 divided by 4 = 10 bags of maize for each bag of fertiliser.
Year 4: she used 6 bags of NPK and harvested 36 bags of maize. That is 36 divided by 6 = 6 bags of maize for each bag of fertiliser.
The return on each bag of fertiliser fell from 10 to 6, a drop of 40 percent, even though she spent more.
Rainfall in both years was normal, so the weather does not explain the drop. Burnt residues, bare soil and no legumes are the likely causes.
Amina's own records show her soil is getting poorer. Her first targets are to stop burning stalks, keep them as mulch and bring cowpea into the rotation, then track the same two numbers next season.

Notice that Amina did not need a laboratory to see the problem. Two numbers written down each year, fertiliser used and harvest, told the story. You will build this habit of simple records throughout the course, because sustainable practices prove themselves slowly and only records show the change.

Testing Your Soil at Home: Texture, Structure, Water Intake and pH
Identify your soil texture using the feel test and the jar test
Measure how fast water soaks into your soil with a simple tin test

Decide when a laboratory soil test is worth paying for

General advice such as "add compost" or "irrigate twice a week" only helps if it fits your soil. A sandy soil drains fast and dries out; a clay soil holds water but can become waterlogged and hard. In this lesson you test your own soil with a bottle, a tin, a ruler and your hands. Do the tests at three or four spots in your field, because soil can change from the top of a slope to the bottom.
A woman studying samples outdoors
Simple home tests tell you most of what you need to know about your soil before spending money.
Test 1: texture by feel

Soil is made of three sizes of mineral particles. **Sand** is the largest and feels gritty. **Silt** is medium and feels smooth like flour. **Clay** is the finest and feels sticky when wet. The mix of the three is called **texture**, and it decides how well soil holds water and nutrients.
Take a small handful of soil from about 15 cm deep and remove stones and roots.
Add water drop by drop and knead until it feels like soft dough.
Squeeze it between thumb and finger, pushing it upwards to make a ribbon.
No ribbon and very gritty: sandy soil. Short ribbon under 2.5 cm: loam. Ribbon 2.5 to 5 cm: clay loam. Long ribbon over 5 cm that is sticky: clay.
Rub a wet pinch in your palm: gritty means more sand, smooth means more silt, sticky means more clay.
Test 2: the jar test

Fill a clear straight-sided bottle or jar about one third with soil. Add water until it is about three quarters full, add a teaspoon of powdered detergent or a few drops of dish soap to help the particles separate, close it and shake hard for three minutes. Set it down where it will not be moved. Sand settles in about one minute, silt within a few hours, and clay can take one or two days. Then measure each layer with a ruler.
Worked example: reading a jar test
For example, Ifeoma in Nsukka shakes soil from her vegetable plot in a clear bottle and measures the layers after two days.
Bottom layer (sand): 3.0 cm. Middle layer (silt): 1.5 cm. Top layer (clay): 1.0 cm. Total: 5.5 cm.
Sand: 3.0 divided by 5.5 = 0.545, about 55 percent.
Silt: 1.5 divided by 5.5 = 0.273, about 27 percent.
Clay: 1.0 divided by 5.5 = 0.182, about 18 percent.
On the standard soil texture triangle, about 55 percent sand, 27 percent silt and 18 percent clay falls in the sandy loam class.
Ifeoma has a sandy loam: easy to work and well drained, but it dries quickly and loses nutrients to heavy rain. Mulch and compost will be her most valuable practices.
Test 3: how fast water soaks in

Remove both ends from a tin such as a tomato paste or milk tin. Push it about 5 cm into moist soil. Pour in water to a level 2.5 cm deep (mark the level inside first) and time how long it takes to disappear. Do it twice in the same spot and use the second time, because the first pour wets dry soil. If water vanishes in a few minutes, the soil drains fast and dries out quickly. If it takes over an hour, the surface is sealed or compacted and rain will run off instead of soaking in. Compare a spot in your field with a spot under a tree or in an old fallow: the difference shows what better soil cover could do.
Test 4: structure and soil life

Dig a block of soil one spade wide and one spade deep, about 20 cm. Break it gently. Good structure crumbles into rounded crumbs of different sizes with many pores and roots. Poor structure comes out as hard flat plates or as loose dust. Now count the earthworms in that block. Many soil guides treat about ten or more earthworms in a spade-sized block as a sign of active soil life, but numbers drop in very dry or very wet weather, so compare spots on the same day and repeat in the same month next year.

Soil pH and when to pay for a lab test

Soil pH measures acidity. Most food crops grow best between about **pH 5.5 and 7.0**. Many soils in humid southern Nigeria are acidic, which locks up phosphorus and can hold back crops even when you add fertiliser. Signs include poor growth despite fertiliser and plants that do better near old ash heaps. Cheap pH test strips and kits exist, but they are rough guides. A laboratory test also reports organic carbon, nitrogen, phosphorus and potassium, and gives a fertiliser and lime recommendation.
Where to get a soil test

Ask your state Agricultural Development Programme (ADP) office, a nearby federal or state university with a soil science department, or an agricultural research institute. Prices vary widely, so ask for the price per sample before you send it. One mixed sample made from 10 to 15 small scoops taken in a zig-zag across one field is better than a single scoop.
Careful with lime and ash

Agricultural lime and wood ash both reduce acidity, but too much can push pH too high and lock up other nutrients. Apply lime only on the advice of a soil test, wear gloves and a dust mask when spreading it, and keep it away from children.

Your soil walk showed what is under your feet. Now map what comes from above and around: water, season length, labour and money. Together they make your **baseline**, the honest picture of your farm today that every later improvement is measured against.
A person checking a weather forecast
Knowing when the rains are expected to start and stop shapes every planting decision.
Map your water

Draw a simple sketch of your farm in your notebook. Mark the slope (which way water runs after rain), any stream, well, borehole, pond or roof that could supply water, and how far each is from your plots. Next to each source write when it dries up. A stream that flows only from June to October is very different from a borehole you can use all year. Note who else depends on the same source, because shared water needs agreement before you plan dry-season vegetables around it.
Know your season

Most Nigerian farming is rain-fed, so the start (onset), end (cessation) and length of the rainy season decide which varieties will finish before the soil dries. Each year the **Nigerian Meteorological Agency (NiMet)** publishes a **Seasonal Climate Prediction (SCP)** with expected onset and cessation dates, season length and possible dry spells for different parts of the country. Your ADP extension officer and many farmer groups share it. Use it together with your own experience: planting after the first single heavy shower, before the rains are steady, is a common way to lose seed.
Keep a rain gauge

A straight-sided tin or plastic container with a flat bottom left in the open works as a simple rain gauge. After each rain, measure the depth of water in millimetres with a ruler, write it down with the date, then empty it. One season of records tells you more about your own farm than any national average.
Count your other resources

Practices differ in what they demand. Crop rotation and seed saving cost mainly planning. Composting and mulching cost labour and access to plant material or manure. A drip kit or water tank costs cash. Write down honestly: how many days a week you and your household can give to the farm, what organic material you can get (crop residues, grass, animal manure, market waste), and what money you could spend this season.

Also note how secure your access to the land is. If you rent a plot for one season at a time, quick practices such as mulch, legumes and planting pits pay back within the season and make sense. Planting trees or building a large compost site makes more sense on land you expect to farm for several years, or where you have a written agreement with the owner or family head. Many women farm land held by a husband or extended family, so talk early with whoever decides, and show them the plan and the expected benefit before you change how the field is used.

Module 1 showed you whether your soil is losing ground. This lesson gives you four low-cost tools to rebuild it: **compost**, **mulch**, **legumes** and **rotation**. None of them needs a shop. They need planning, some labour and the plant material and manure that are already around most farms.
A woman tending plants in a garden bed
Compost, mulch and legumes turn farm waste into fertility that stays in your soil.
Making compost that works

Compost is plant and animal waste that soil organisms have broken down into a dark, crumbly material. It feeds soil life, slowly releases nutrients and helps sandy soil hold water and clay soil drain. A good heap balances two kinds of material. **Greens** are fresh and rich in nitrogen: fresh leaves, vegetable peels, fresh grass, and poultry, goat or cow manure. **Browns** are dry and rich in carbon: dry maize stalks cut short, dry leaves, straw, rice husks and sawdust from untreated wood. A common guide is about two to three parts browns to one part greens by volume.
Choose a shaded spot near water. In dry areas dig a pit about 50 cm deep; in wet areas build a heap on the ground so it does not waterlog.
Lay a base of coarse sticks or stalks about 15 cm deep so air can enter from below.
Add layers: about 15 to 20 cm of browns, then 5 to 10 cm of greens and manure, then a thin sprinkle of old soil or compost to bring in soil organisms.
Water each layer until it is moist like a squeezed-out sponge, not dripping.
Build it to about 1 m wide and 1 m high so it can heat up, then cover with leaves, sacks or old roofing sheet against sun and heavy rain.
After a week, push a stick or cutlass into the centre for a minute. It should come out warm. Turn the heap every one to two weeks, moving outside material to the middle and adding water if dry.
Compost is ready when it is dark and crumbly, smells of earth and you can no longer recognise the starting materials, often after about two to three months with regular turning in warm weather.
Handling manure and compost safely

Manure can carry germs that cause illness. Wear gloves or wash hands well with soap after handling it, and keep cuts covered. Never use human, dog or cat faeces. Use only well-made compost or well-rotted manure on vegetables eaten raw, and do not add meat, bones, oily food, plastic or diseased plants to the heap.
Worked example: how much compost for a vegetable bed?
For example, Blessing in Ibadan has a raised bed 1.2 m wide and 8 m long for tomatoes. Her extension officer suggests working about 3 cm of compost into the top of the bed before planting.
Bed area: 1.2 m x 8 m = 9.6 square metres.
Compost depth: 3 cm = 0.03 m.
Volume: 9.6 x 0.03 = 0.288 cubic metres. One cubic metre is 1,000 litres, so she needs about 288 litres.
In 20-litre buckets: 288 divided by 20 = 14.4, so about 15 buckets.
A fresh heap 1.5 m x 1.5 m x 1 m holds 2.25 cubic metres of material. Heaps commonly shrink to about half as they decompose, leaving roughly 1.1 cubic metres, about 1,100 litres.
One well-built heap gives Blessing about 1,100 litres, enough for 1,100 divided by 288 = about 3.8 beds of this size. She plans one heap for every three to four beds.
Mulch: a blanket for your soil

Mulch is any material laid on the soil surface: dry grass, maize or sorghum stalks, rice straw, leaves or groundnut haulms. It shades the soil, stops raindrops from smashing the surface into a crust, slows evaporation, keeps roots cooler and smothers many weeds. As it breaks down it feeds soil life. Spread a layer about 5 to 10 cm thick after the soil is moist, and keep it a few centimetres away from plant stems to prevent rot. Termites may eat some mulch in dry areas; that is normal, but top it up and keep it away from young stems.
Legumes and rotation

Legumes such as cowpea, groundnut, soybean, bambara nut and pigeon pea carry rhizobia in root nodules that fix nitrogen from the air. Cut a healthy nodule open during flowering: pink or red inside means it is actively fixing nitrogen. Growing a legume before or alongside a cereal can reduce the nitrogen the cereal needs from fertiliser, especially when legume leaves and haulms are returned to the soil. Cover crops such as mucuna (velvet bean) or lablab can also be grown after the main crop or in a fallow to cover the soil, add organic matter and suppress weeds.

Rotation means changing the crop family on each plot each season. It breaks the life cycles of pests and diseases that attack one family, and different crops take nutrients from different depths. A key rule: do not follow tomato with pepper, garden egg or Irish potato, because they belong to the same family and share diseases such as bacterial wilt.

Water problems on small farms come in two forms. In the rainy season, rain falls hard and runs off before it soaks in. In dry spells and the dry season, there is not enough water and what there is gets wasted. The answer is to **catch rain where it falls, keep it in the soil, and deliver irrigation only where roots can use it**.
A person watering young plants
Every litre that reaches the roots instead of running off or evaporating is a litre saved.
Catch rain in the field

**Planting pits (zai pits):** a traditional Sahel technique. Dig pits roughly 20 to 40 cm across and 10 to 20 cm deep, put a handful or two of compost or manure in each and plant in them. They collect runoff and concentrate nutrients around the roots, and are most useful on crusted, degraded soils in drier areas.
**Half-moons:** crescent-shaped earth bunds, open side facing uphill, that trap water running down a gentle slope. Plant inside the curve.
**Tied ridges:** ordinary ridges with small cross-ties every few metres, making a grid of basins that hold rain in place instead of letting it flow down the furrow.
**Contour planting:** ridges, rows and grass strips laid across the slope, never up and down it, so water slows and soaks in.
**Mulch and residues:** from the last lesson, they cut crusting and evaporation at almost no cost.
Store water from roofs

A useful fact: **1 mm of rain on 1 square metre gives 1 litre of water**. Multiply the roof area by the rainfall in millimetres, then by a runoff factor of about 0.8 for a metal roof, because some water splashes, evaporates or is lost in gutters. Fit a mesh at the tank inlet and divert the first few minutes of each rain away from the tank, since it carries dust and droppings from the roof.
Worked example: tank or drip, how far will the water go?

For example, Grace in Jos has a metal roof 6 m by 8 m, a 1,000-litre tank and a 100 square metre tomato plot for the dry season. For this example, her extension officer estimates the crop needs about 4 mm of water a day at its peak.
Roof area: 6 x 8 = 48 square metres. One 25 mm rain gives 48 x 25 x 0.8 = 960 litres, so one good rain nearly fills the tank.
Net water the crop needs: 4 mm x 100 square metres = 400 litres per day.
FAO training manuals use indicative field application efficiencies of about 60 percent for surface irrigation and 90 percent for drip.
Surface or watering can: 400 divided by 0.60 = about 667 litres per day.
Drip: 400 divided by 0.90 = about 444 litres per day, a saving of about 222 litres every day (666.7 minus 444.4).
Over 60 days of peak demand, drip saves about 222 x 60 = 13,320 litres.

A full tank covers just over 2 days of drip irrigation at peak. Grace uses the tank for her nursery and early weeks, and plans a borehole share or shallow well for the full dry-season crop, with drip lines to make that water go further.

Small drip systems

A family drip kit is a tank raised on a stand about 1 m or more above the bed, a filter, a main pipe and thin drip lines with small emitters beside each plant. Gravity does the work, so no pump or power is needed. Clean the filter every few days, flush the line ends weekly, and check that each emitter drips, because blocked emitters are the most common reason a crop dries out unevenly. Lay mulch over the lines to cut evaporation further.
Water at the right time and amount

**Integrated pest management (IPM)** means using several methods together to keep pests below the level that costs you money, while protecting your health, beneficial insects and the soil. It replaces spraying on a fixed calendar with a simple routine: prevent, watch, decide, then act with the least harmful option that works.
A ladybird beetle
Ladybirds and their larvae eat aphids; careless spraying kills these free helpers first.

Most of the work sits at the wide base; chemicals belong at the narrow top and only when scouting shows they are needed.
Step 1: prevent
Rotate crop families so pests and diseases cannot build up in the same plot
Use certified or well-selected clean seed and resistant varieties where available
Plant at the right time and spacing; stressed, crowded plants attract pests
Remove and destroy badly diseased plants and crop debris that carry pests between seasons
Keep field edges with flowering plants that shelter ladybirds, hoverflies and parasitic wasps
Step 2: scout and measure

Walk the field once or twice a week in a W pattern, stopping at five places away from the edge. At each stop check a fixed number of plants, for example 20, and count those with fresh damage or live pests. Record the date and the count. The percentage tells you whether the problem is growing, and comparing with your extension officer's advice tells you when to act.
Know your enemy: fall armyworm

Fall armyworm, a caterpillar originally from the Americas, was first reported in West and Central Africa in 2016, including Nigeria, and now attacks maize in most seasons. Look for small windowpane patches on young leaves, ragged holes, and wet sawdust-like droppings (frass) in the funnel (whorl) of the plant. The larva has a pale upside-down Y on its head and four dark dots forming a square near its tail end. Young larvae are easiest to control, so early scouting matters.
Worked example: to act or to wait?

For example, Bisi grows 0.5 hectare of maize in Oyo State. Her ADP officer advised her to take action against fall armyworm if fresh whorl damage passes 20 percent of young plants. This action level is an example; ask your own officer for advice for your crop and stage.
Week 3 after planting: 5 stops x 20 plants = 100 plants checked. 12 have fresh damage: 12 divided by 100 = 12 percent.
Below 20 percent, so she crushes egg masses and young larvae by hand on damaged plants and scouts again in 4 days.
Week 4: 100 plants checked, 27 with fresh damage = 27 percent, now above the action level.
She chooses a targeted option recommended by her officer and registered for maize, applied into the whorls of affected areas rather than blanket spraying the whole field.
Week 5: fresh damage falls to 8 percent, so she returns to scouting only.
Bisi treated once, at the right time and in the right place, instead of spraying every week. She saved money and protected the natural enemies that keep pests down between treatments.
Step 3: physical and biological options

Hand-picking, removing infested plant parts and traps work well on small plots. **Push-pull**, developed by icipe (the International Centre of Insect Physiology and Ecology) with partners, plants the legume Desmodium between maize rows to push stemborer moths and fall armyworm away, and a border of Napier or Brachiaria grass to pull them out of the crop. Desmodium also suppresses the parasitic Striga weed and adds nitrogen. Botanical sprays such as neem seed extract are widely used by smallholders; a common recipe soaks about 50 g of ground neem seed kernels per litre of water overnight, then filters it. Botanicals are milder, but still wear gloves and wash hands after use.
Step 4: if you must use a pesticide
Recognised pesticide safety rules

Buy only from a registered agro-dealer, in the original sealed container with a NAFDAC registration number on the label. Read the label: which crop and pest it is approved for, the protective clothing needed, the re-entry interval and the pre-harvest interval (days to wait before harvest). Never mix or exceed the label rate. Wear gloves, long sleeves, trousers, boots and eye protection; spray in calm, cool weather, never into the wind; do not eat, drink or smoke while working, and wash well afterwards. Pregnant or breastfeeding women and children should not mix or spray. Store pesticides locked away from food, water and children, never in drink bottles. Triple-rinse empty containers into the sprayer, puncture them and never reuse them for food or water. If someone feels ill after exposure, go to a health facility at once and take the label with you.

Keep a spray record: date, product, plot, amount mixed, weather and the date when harvest is safe. Buyers and food processors increasingly ask about pesticide use, and the record protects you if a question about residues ever comes up.

Rainfall in many parts of Nigeria is becoming harder to predict: late onsets, long dry spells in the middle of the season and heavy storms that wash soil away. **Climate-smart agriculture**, as FAO describes it, has three goals: raise productivity and incomes sustainably, help farms adapt and recover from climate shocks, and reduce greenhouse gas emissions where possible. On a small farm the first two come first, and the practices you learned in Module 2 already serve both.

Climate-smart options to consider

**Drought-tolerant and early-maturing varieties:** research centres such as IITA have worked with national partners to release maize and cowpea varieties that cope better with dry spells or finish before the rains end. Ask your ADP or a registered seed company which certified varieties suit your zone.
**Planting dates from the forecast:** use NiMet's Seasonal Climate Prediction and your rain gauge to plant once the rains are established, and stagger plantings a week or two apart to spread risk.

**Trees on the farm (agroforestry):** boundary trees and windbreaks reduce wind damage and drying. In the drier north, Faidherbia albida is valued because it drops its leaves in the rainy season, so it does not shade the crop, and its leaf fall adds organic matter.
**Diversify:** a mix of crops, and small livestock such as goats or poultry whose manure feeds the compost heap, spreads risk if one crop fails.
**Keep soil covered and water stored:** mulch, legumes, pits and tanks are climate-smart because they protect yields in bad years.
Why you need a fair trial

A neighbour says her mulched maize did better. Was it the mulch, or did she also plant earlier, use a new variety and get more rain? The only way to know what works on **your** land is a **side-by-side trial**: two plots, side by side, treated exactly the same except for the one practice you are testing.

For example, Hauwa from Module 1 runs a mulch trial on two 100 square metre maize plots. For this example, she values a day of labour at about 3,000 naira and maize grain at about 700 naira per kg; both are approximate and vary by place and season.

Extra cost: 1 day collecting and spreading mulch = 3,000 naira (approximate).

Why this matters
Put back what each harvest takes out
Each harvest removes nutrients from your soil
Burning and bare soil make it poorer
Soil life works for free when protected
Not a costly system: a set of habits
Sustainable farming keeps your land able to feed you next year, and when your children take over. Every bag of maize you carry away holds nutrients that came from your soil.
When stalks are burnt and nothing is returned, the soil gets poorer each season. Rain washes bare topsoil away, and the sun burns off organic matter, the dark crumbly remains that hold water.
Soil is alive. Rhizobia bacteria on the roots of cowpea, groundnut and soybean turn nitrogen from the air into plant food. Fungi help roots reach water.
This is not a costly system. It is a set of habits.
FAO's three principles
Conservation agriculture
Dig only where and when you must. Plant in rows or holes, and avoid burning before planting.
Keep the ground covered with crops, residues or mulch. Leave maize stalks on the surface.
Rotate crop families. Follow maize with cowpea or groundnut, or intercrop cassava with a legume.
The FAO describes three linked principles. First, minimum soil disturbance, so soil structure and soil life are not destroyed.
Second, permanent soil cover for most of the year.
Third, crop diversification. And sustainable does not mean no fertiliser. It means every bag works harder.
Worked example
Amina's two numbers
Year 1
4 bags of NPK used
40 bags of maize harvested
10 bags of maize per bag
Year 4
6 bags of NPK used
36 bags of maize harvested
6 bags of maize per bag

For example, Amina farms 1 hectare of maize near Zaria and burns the stalks every dry season. In year 1 she used 4 bags of NPK and harvested 40 bags. That is 10 bags of maize for each bag of fertiliser.
In year 4 she used 6 bags and harvested 36. Only 6 bags of maize per bag of fertiliser, a drop of 40 percent, with normal rain.
Two numbers written each year told the story. She will stop burning, keep stalks as mulch and bring in cowpea.
Test your soil at home
Fill a clear jar one third with soil
Add water to three quarters, plus soap
Shake hard for three minutes
Wait one or two days
Measure each layer with a ruler
Soil is a mix of gritty sand, smooth silt and sticky clay. The mix decides how your soil holds water. Step one. Fill a clear, straight-sided jar about one third with soil.
Step two. Add water until it is three quarters full, and a few drops of dish soap to separate the particles.
Step three. Close it and shake hard for three minutes.
Step four. Leave it still. Sand settles in a minute, silt in a few hours, clay in one or two days.

Step five. Measure the layers. For example, Ifeoma in Nsukka got about 55 percent sand, 27 percent silt and 18 percent clay. That is a sandy loam: easy to work, but it dries quickly, so mulch and compost will help her most.
More quick tests
Water, structure, life and pH
Tin test: time 2.5 cm of water to soak in
Spade block: rounded crumbs, not plates
Count earthworms in the block
Most crops like pH 5.5 to 7.0
Push an open-ended tin about 5 cm into moist soil, pour in water 2.5 cm deep and time it. Use the second pour. Over an hour means the surface is sealed and rain will run off.
Dig a spade-sized block about 20 cm deep. Good soil crumbles into rounded crumbs. Poor soil comes out as hard plates or dust.
Count the earthworms. About ten or more is a sign of active soil life. Test three spots, top, middle and bottom of any slope.
Many southern soils are acidic. If fertiliser stops working, pay for a lab test through your ADP office or a university.
Safety first
Lime only on a soil test's advice
Too much pushes pH too high
Wear gloves and a dust mask
Keep lime away from children
Lime and wood ash reduce acidity, but too much locks up other nutrients. Apply lime only on a soil test's advice. Wear gloves and a dust mask when spreading it, and keep it away from children.

Step by step
Building a compost heap
Never use human, dog or cat faeces. Wash hands after manure.
Shaded spot; pit in dry areas, heap in wet
Base of coarse sticks, about 15 cm
Layers: browns, greens and manure, old soil
Moist like a squeezed-out sponge
About 1 m wide and 1 m high, covered
Turn every one to two weeks
Compost needs greens, which are fresh, like peels and manure, and browns, which are dry, like stalks and dry leaves. Use about two to three parts browns to one part greens.
Step one. Choose a shaded spot near water.
Step two. Lay coarse sticks about 15 cm deep, so air enters from below.
Step three. Add browns, then greens and manure, then a sprinkle of old soil to bring in soil organisms.
Step four. Water each layer until moist, not dripping.
Step five. Build it about 1 m wide and 1 m high, and cover it against sun and heavy rain.
Step six. After a week, push a stick into the centre. Warm means it is working. Turn it every one to two weeks. It is ready in about two to three months.
Manure can carry germs, so wear gloves or wash well with soap.
Free fertility
Mulch, legumes and rotation
Mulch 5 to 10 cm thick, off the stems
Legumes fix nitrogen: pink nodules
Rotate crop families every season
Never tomato after pepper or garden egg
Mulch is a blanket of dry grass, stalks or leaves. It stops crusting, slows evaporation and smothers weeds. Spread it 5 to 10 cm thick, away from stems.
Legumes such as cowpea, groundnut and soybean fix nitrogen. Cut a nodule open at flowering. Pink or red inside means it is working.
Rotate: cereal, then legume, then fruit vegetable, then a leaf or root crop.
And never follow tomato with pepper, garden egg or Irish potato. They are one family and share diseases like bacterial wilt.
Saving water
Catch rain where it falls
Planting pits with compost in each
Half-moons, open side facing uphill
Tied ridges: small basins hold rain
Rows and ridges across the slope
Roof water: 1 mm on 1 m² = 1 litre
Catch rain where it falls. Planting pits, about 20 to 40 cm across with compost in each, collect runoff around the roots.
Half-moons trap water running down a gentle slope.
Tied ridges have small cross-ties every few metres, making basins that hold rain in place.
Lay rows and ridges across the slope, never up and down it.

From a metal roof, multiply the area by the rain in millimetres, then by 0.8. For example, Grace in Jos has a 48 square metre roof. One 25 mm rain gives about 960 litres, nearly filling her 1,000-litre tank.
Worked example
Grace's tomatoes: watering can or drip?
Surface watering
About 667 litres a day
About 444 litres a day
Saves 13,320 litres in 60 days
Grace's 100 square metre tomato plot needs about 400 litres a day at its peak. With a watering can, only about 60 percent reaches the roots, so she must carry about 667 litres.
Drip delivers about 90 percent, so 444 litres is enough. Over 60 days that saves about 13,320 litres.
Before watering, squeeze a handful of soil from the root zone. Water only if it crumbles dry.
Safety first
Cover every tank, drum and pot
Fence or cover ponds and deep pits
Never leave children alone near water
No sewage water on raw-eaten vegetables

Cover every tank and drum with a lid or mesh so mosquitoes cannot breed. Fence open ponds and deep pits and never leave children alone near them. And never use untreated sewage or drainage water on vegetables eaten raw.
Pest management
Scout before you spray
Prevent: rotation, clean seed, spacing
Walk a W pattern, five stops, 20 plants
Work out the percentage damaged
Below the action level: act by hand
Above it: targeted option, last resort
Integrated pest management means prevent, watch, decide, then act with the least harmful option. Prevention comes first.
Once or twice a week, walk the field in a W pattern. At five stops, check 20 plants. For fall armyworm on maize, look for windowpane patches and sawdust-like droppings in the whorl.
For example, Bisi in Oyo State found 12 damaged plants out of 100. That is 12 percent.
Her officer's action level was 20 percent, so she crushed eggs and young larvae by hand and scouted again.
The next week it was 27 percent. She used one targeted option, registered for maize, only into the affected whorls. By week 5, damage fell to 8 percent. One treatment, not weekly spraying.
If you must spray
Pesticide safety rules
Registered dealer, sealed, NAFDAC number
Read the label; never exceed the rate
Gloves, long sleeves, boots, eye cover
Calm weather, never into the wind
No mixing or spraying if pregnant
Locked away; never in drink bottles
Buy only from a registered agro-dealer, with a NAFDAC number on the label. Read the label, including the days to wait before harvest. Wear full protection and never spray into the wind.
Pregnant or breastfeeding women and children should not mix or spray. Store pesticides locked away, and if someone feels ill, go to a health facility with the label.
Key points
Remember
Compost: browns, greens, air, water, turning
Mulch thick; include a legume every cycle
Catch rain with pits, ridges and roofs
Drip stretches water much further
Scout first; chemicals last and safely
To remember. Build compost with browns and greens. Mulch, and bring a legume into every cycle. Catch rain where it falls. Use drip to stretch water. And scout first, with chemicals last.

Climate-smart choices
Spread your climate risk
Drought-tolerant, early-maturing varieties
Plant once the rains are established
Trees as windbreaks and boundaries
Mix crops, and small livestock
Keep soil covered and water stored
Rainfall is getting harder to predict. Climate-smart farming helps you produce more and recover from shocks. Ask your ADP which certified drought-tolerant or early-maturing varieties suit your zone.
Use NiMet's forecast and your rain gauge, and stagger plantings a week or two apart.
Boundary trees and windbreaks reduce wind damage and drying.
A mix of crops, plus goats or poultry whose manure feeds the compost, spreads risk if one crop fails.
And mulch, legumes, pits and tanks from Module 2 protect yields in bad years.
Step by step
Running a fair side-by-side trial
Change one thing only. Keep everything else the same.
Choose one change to test
Mark two equal plots, side by side
Same variety, date, spacing, weeding
Write the plan before planting
Weekly notes: height, wilting, pests
Weigh each harvest separately

A neighbour says her mulched maize did better. But was it the mulch, or did she also plant earlier and use a new variety? A fair trial tells you what works on your land. Step one. Choose one change, for example mulch or no mulch.
Step two. Mark two plots of the same size on similar soil, for example 10 m by 10 m each, with pegs and string.
Step three. Treat both exactly the same, except the one practice you are testing.
Step four. Label the plots and write the plan in your notebook before planting.
Steps five and six. Note crop height, wilting and pests every week. Then harvest and weigh each plot separately, and compare per square metre.
Worked example
Did Hauwa's mulch pay?
For example, Hauwa compares two 100 square metre maize plots, mulched and unmulched.
12 kg extra grain at 700 per kg
Extra cost: 1 day of labour
Naira prices are approximate.
The mulched plot gave 52 kg of dry grain. The unmulched plot gave 40 kg. That is 0.52 against 0.40 kg per square metre, 30 percent more.
At about 700 naira per kg, the extra 12 kg is worth 8,400 naira.
Collecting and spreading mulch took 1 day, valued at about 3,000 naira.
So her net gain on 100 square metres is about 5,400 naira. Because one season can mislead, she will repeat the trial next year.
And be honest. If a plot is spoilt by goats or late weeding, record it, and never stretch one good result into a promise to neighbours.
Getting support
Ask your extension officer well
Vague request
Help me farm better
No numbers, no photo
Easy to forget
Specific request
Water took over an hour to soak in
Maize wilts after a week dry
Which variety? Visit in July?
Your state ADP, NAERLS, research institutes like IITA, and farmer groups can all help. But extension officers cover many farmers, and a vague request is easy to forget.

Use your own numbers. My sandy loam took over an hour to absorb water, and my maize wilts after one week without rain. Can you advise a drought-tolerant variety and visit my trial in July? Send it with a photo, and follow up politely.
Sharing what works
Ask before adding anyone to a group or sharing their photo.

Farmers trust what they see on a neighbour's farm. For example, Ngozi near Awka invited 15 women to her compost and mulch plots on a Saturday after market. Water, snacks and picture sheets cost about 9,000 naira. Start with a welcome and the problem.
Walk the two plots, so people see the difference.
Share your numbers.
Then let everyone try it. Ngozi's group built a small compost heap together.
End with questions. Collect names and numbers only with permission, and keep the list safe. And never call produce organic unless you can show it.
Keep the evidence
Indicators to track every season
Water intake time at the same spots
Earthworm count, same spots and month
Days the crop survives a dry spell

Your capstone is an evidence pack: baseline, practices, trial records, results, lessons and a plan. Track the same indicators each year. Yield per square metre and harvest per bag of fertiliser should rise.
Water should soak in faster, and you should find more earthworms.
Sprays should fall, and your crop should survive dry spells longer. Grace in Jos found her mulched maize gave about 22 percent more, and honestly noted a compost heap that stayed cold.
Three months, three goals
Prepare materials and land. For example, build two new compost heaps and collect mulch.
Extend the practice that worked to more land, or add a second practice on a trial plot.
Hold a field day or group visit, and review your records against the indicators.
Break your plan into three months. Days 1 to 30, prepare.
Days 31 to 60, scale up what worked.
Days 61 to 90, share and review. For each step, write the date, the number you aim for and the partner involved. Keep it to one page with up to three photos.
Key points
Remember
Varieties, timing, trees and diversity
A fair trial changes one thing only
Compare per square metre and net gain
Ask for help with your own numbers
Record results honestly, then repeat
To remember. Spread your climate risk. Test one change at a time. Compare per square metre and net gain. Ask for help with your own numbers. And record results honestly, then repeat.
